What truly lasts is the ability to break workflows into system components with clear boundaries that are composable, observable, and revertible. Skill is exactly such an entry point—small enough to start with a single file, low enough of a threshold that you can write in Markdown. But once it enters a real workflow, it brings out a range of engineering concerns: context, tools, permissions, evaluation, versioning, and governance. The shift from "writing prompts" to "designing workflows" means engineering teams must start answering: which experiences are worth codifying, which rules stay resident and which load on demand, which judgments go to the model and which actions go to scripts, which flows need checkpoints, which Skills can auto-update and which need human review, and whether old Skills still fit after model upgrades. This question framework matters more than the Skills themselves, because it defines the methodology for how a team continuously evolves Agent capabilities.
